title: MemCoRe: Recovering Evidence from Progressively Compressed Factual Knowledge for Agent Memory
claim: Organize memory as a nested compression hierarchy, built incrementally from inputs and searched across levels by a multi-route retrieval pipeline.
layout: 3 columns: construction flow left, concentric hierarchy center, retrieval flow right
description: The figure has three parts. On the left, a vertical Memory Construction flow starts with input blocks x1 to xt. These go through Semantic Ingestion, then a dashed box of icons (raw, context, keywords, embedding), then an LLM gate diamond. The gate branches into Merge, Link and Append, grouped under a 'Build relations' brace. In the center, concentric circles show the hierarchy. The outer green ring holds Topics (1), the middle purple ring holds Keywords (2), and the inner orange circle holds Notes (3) as a graph of linked nodes. Curved arrows labeled cluster and extract link the levels. Below the circles is the formula min I(X;M) − βI(M,Q;T). On the right, Memory Retrieval runs from Query q to a Semantic Parser. The parser fans out into three colored routes (Topics, Keywords, Neighbors) that enter the hierarchy and merge in RRF Fusion. The flow then goes through Iter to Answer. The eye goes first to the colorful central rings. The figure shown is an architecture diagram, so it does not match the caption's diagnostic plots.
caption: Diagnostic analysis on LoCoMo (A-MEM, Qwen3-8B). (a) Per-category top-20 retrieval recall; 28.2% of results are near-duplicates. (b) Downstream F1 when target evidence is diluted to 100%/50%/10% of the retrieved context. Setup details in Appendix [ref].
abstract: Memory systems enable LLM agents to consolidate and retrieve relevant evidence from the factual knowledge accumulated through growing interaction histories for downstream reasoning. Existing approaches have explored diverse strategies for organizing and compressing these histories. However, balancing compression with retrieval effectiveness remains challenging: retaining too much content can cause relevant evidence to be obscured by redundant entries, while discarding too aggressively may remove content that later proves relevant. This amounts to a tradeoff between compressing redundancy and preserving enough structure to retrieve target evidence, as formalized by the information bottleneck. To this end, we propose MemCoRe, which organizes memory as a compression hierarchy where each level compresses redundancy further while retaining the structure needed for retrieval at that level. In this hierarchy, evidence is progressively compressed from detailed records through extracted keywords to topic groups. This enables retrieval to locate target evidence by searching across levels of the hierarchy. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that MemCoRe outperforms existing state-of-the-art baselines.
